meta.title: Who really said "If people don't want to come to the ballpark, how are you going to stop them?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wikiquote files this wording under Disputed: the joke is in print in 1952 from impresario Sol Hurok, a decade before it was first tied to Yogi Berra.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If people don't want to come to the ballpark, how are you going to stop them?'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Yogi original. Sol Hurok was quoted with the joke in 1952; this exact ballpark wording comes from Berra's own book, decades later.

answer.label: Not originally Yogi Berra — the joke starts with Sol Hurok
answer.sourceLine: This exact ballpark wording really is Berra’s — it is printed in his own The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!, which is the citation Wikiquote attaches to it, at page 36. But the joke was not his to invent. On August 16, 1952 the columnist Leonard Lyons quoted the concert impresario Sol Hurok: “If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” The earliest citation linking any version of the gag to Berra is from 1962, and Wikiquote files this line under Disputed for exactly that reason.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed: the ballpark phrasing is Berra’s own published wording, but the joke is documented from Sol Hurok a decade before anyone hung it on Yogi.

source.excerpt: I’m enough of a showman to have learned at least this: If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.
source.trailTitle: How a showman’s line became a baseball line
trail: 1952 — Leonard Lyons’ column of August 16 in The Post-Standard (Syracuse, NY) quotes Sol Hurok: “If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” This is the earliest instance the specialists have found. Quote Investigator ↗

1959 — LIFE magazine of June 1 runs Joseph Roddy’s Hurok profile, “Impresario Who Booked the Bolshoi,” which carries the line again in the present tense: “When people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” Quote Investigator ↗

1962–1963 — Joe Garagiola tells a New Orleans banquet on September 13, 1962 that his boyhood friend Yogi said, of the sagging Kansas City gate, “If they don’t want to come out, nobody’s gonna stop ’em.” A year later he glosses it for Arthur Daley of The New York Times: Yogi “merely was saying that no one could force spectators to attend.” Quote Investigator ↗

1998 — Workman publishes The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! in New York Open Library catalogue record ↗. That book, at page 36, is the source Wikiquote cites for the exact wording on this page — and it still lists the line under Disputed ↗.
source.excerptNote: Sol Hurok, warning the producers of his film biography Tonight We Sing, as quoted by Leonard Lyons on August 16, 1952. Note what is not here: no ballpark, and no “how are you going to stop them.” Those are Berra’s, and in this phrasing they arrive decades later.

author.name: Sol Hurok
author.kicker: The man the joke actually starts with
author.heading: Who was Sol Hurok?
author.bio: Sol Hurok was the twentieth century’s most famous concert impresario — the man behind the “S. Hurok Presents” billing that carried Marian Anderson, Arthur Rubinstein and a parade of Russian dancers onto American stages. Born in the Russian Empire on April 9, 1888, he emigrated to the United States in 1906 and was naturalised in 1914; he arranged Anderson’s landmark Lincoln Memorial concert in 1939 and, after decades of trying, brought the Bolshoi Ballet to America in 1959. He talked about the box office with the fatalism of a man who had spent fifty years selling tickets: you can advertise, you can beg, you cannot make people show up.

misattribution.heading: Berra said it. Hurok said it first.
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication. Yogi Berra really did say versions of this line, and this particular phrasing is printed in his own book. It is a priority problem: the joke was already in circulation under someone else’s name a decade before anyone tied it to Yogi.

items.why: The exact sentence on this page is cited by Wikiquote ↗ to The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! at page 36 — and Wikiquote still files it under Disputed, because of what came before it.

Leonard Lyons’ column of August 16, 1952 quotes the impresario warning the producers of his own film biography: “If people don’t want to come, nothing will stop them.” A June 1959 LIFE profile carries it again, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Berra’s boyhood friend and fellow catcher-turned-broadcaster was the one telling the story from podiums. A September 13, 1962 Times-Picayune report of his banquet speech is the earliest link of the gag to Yogi; in October 1963 he explained it to Arthur Daley of The New York Times. See Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the ballpark words are Berra’s, but the joke is Sol Hurok’s — in print in 1952, a decade before it was first attached to Yogi. Quote Investigator names Hurok the originator ↗.

context.heading: Why this one keeps getting pinned on Yogi
lead: Yogi Berra is one of the internet’s great quote magnets, and he knew it — the subtitle of his own quotation book is I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!. An attendance joke drifts toward him almost automatically, because the shape of the line is the shape of every Yogi-ism: a sentence that reads like a tautology until you hear the shrug inside it.

But this one had a previous owner. Sol Hurok spent half a century selling seats for singers and ballet companies, and the fatalism is his: you can advertise, you can paper the house, you cannot make people show up. What Berra did was move it from the concert hall to the ballpark — in the 1960s citations, specifically to the thin crowds watching the Athletics in Kansas City.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology runs: Leonard Lyons’ column of August 16, 1952 in The Post-Standard of Syracuse, quoting Hurok on his own film biography Tonight We Sing; Joseph Roddy’s LIFE profile of June 1, 1959, “Impresario Who Booked the Bolshoi,” which reprises the line; then, on September 13, 1962, a Times-Picayune report of Joe Garagiola addressing a “Banquet of Champions” for young ballplayers, passing on his friend Yogi’s quip about the sagging Kansas City attendance. A 1963 Celebrity Register entry for Hurok carries the showman’s version yet again.

Berra himself was open about it. In When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It!, written with David Kaplan and published by Hyperion in 2001, he wrote that he thought he first said it about the poor attendance in Kansas City, and that he said something like it again to Bud Selig during Selig’s spell as interim commissioner, when the gate was falling under the threat of a strike. He was, in other words, describing a line he had reused — not one he had coined.

The clipped question form on this page — “how are you going to stop them?” — is the version that ended up on mugs and t-shirts. It does not appear in any of the mid-century newspaper citations; the source Wikiquote gives for it is Berra’s own The Yogi Book, page 36, in the Workman edition Wikiquote dates to 1997 (Open Library catalogues the Workman printing as New York, 1998).
context.pull: You can advertise, you can beg. You cannot make people show up.
